One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
From what we eat to how much we move, even how we sleep ... scientists are suggesting that the power to push back Alzheimer's disease is largely in our hands.

Unique Selling Point:
Alzheimer's is the most common form of dementia, accounting for up to 70 per cent of cases. From what we eat to how much we move, even how we sleep ... scientists are suggesting that the power to push back the disease is largely in our hands.

Press Release:


Alzheimer’s: Can we Prevent it?
It’s said memory is the mother of all wisdom, a fundamental part of being human. But, the most common form of dementia—Alzheimer’s disease—accounts for up to 70 percent of cases. And, after the age of 65, the chance of getting the disease doubles every five years. There is no cure, only the prospect of the cruel and undignified descent. But mounting research suggests that Alzheimer's can be delayed and even prevented. Carte Blanche explores the lifestyle choices—from what we eat to how much we move, even how we sleep—that may affect our chances of cognitive decline in the future. Is the power to push back the disease largely in our hands?
Producer: Dr Geraldine McKenna


Script:


NARRATION
It's said memory is the mother of all wisdom, a fundamental part of being human. But Alzheimer's disease slowly robs the mind. It's a cruel and undignified descent.

Prof Cassandra Szoeke
We know that every five years after the age of 65, your chance of getting dementia doubles. And that's very scary.

NARRATION
Currently, there is no cure. But mounting research suggests that Alzheimer's can be delayed - and even prevented.

Prof Cassandra Szoeke
It's absolutely possible to have a healthy older age with intact memory and cognitive function.

NARRATION
In this episode, we explore how our lifestyle choices today might affect our chances of cognitive decline in the future.

Prof Kirk Erickson
One year of brisk walking was enough to roll back the ageing clock by about one to two years.

Prof Cassandra Szoeke
Those who were adhering to a Mediterranean diet had better cognition over time.

NARRATION
From what we eat to how much we move, even how we sleep, scientists are suggesting that the power to push back the disease is largely in our hands.

Prof Ralph Martins
I honestly believe that probably as much as 80% of Alzheimer's is preventable.

Graham Plant
(referring to a photo) That was probably about...I'd say my 16th birthday or so. Pretty standard for our house. There's cakes that Mum's made on there, and there's a bottle of beer, which is the old man's, I'm guessing, on the table.

NARRATION
Graham Plant grew up in country Victoria. As a young man, he was close to his mum, Cathy.

Graham Plant
She lived for the family and the kids, and that was what really drove her, and she was happiest when the family was around her.

NARRATION
But about 10 years ago, Cathy Plant developed Alzheimer's. She was in her late 60s.

Graham Plant
It was kind of a slow onset, and then as it got slightly worse, she started to forget things that she was good at, like cooking, or she'd just forget to do things altogether, or she just got disoriented. Like putting the electric kettle on the hotplate, and things like that, and forgetting what can go in the oven and what can't, and those sort of things. When people get diagnosed with dementia, Alzheimer's, you lose them long before they go. That's kind of the way it is.

NARRATION
Alzheimer's disease is the most common form of dementia, accounting for up to 70% of cases. The condition is chronic, degenerative and ultimately terminal.

Prof Cassandra Szoeke
So, the hallmarks of the disease, clinically speaking, is memory loss and change in brain function. For some of the dementias, this can be other brain functions than memory, but for Alzheimer's disease, the first changes noticed are memory.

NARRATION
In a healthy brain, billions of neurons send messages to each other via electrical or chemical signals down a long tail - an axon. These are the synaptic connections through which messages travel. But in the Alzheimer's brain, toxic deposits accumulate, including a protein called beta-amyloid. The amyloid seems to attract another brain protein called tau to form fibrous clumps inside brain cells. This disturbs the brain's message transport system and neural networks effectively disintegrate.
Until recently, this characteristic accumulation of beta-amyloid was only detectable after death in a post-mortem. But thanks largely to Australian research, with advanced imaging, it can now be seen in the living. It turns out the process of accumulation can begin several decades before Alzheimer's disease appears.

Prof Cassandra Szoeke
To get from a normal amount to the amount in people with Alzheimer's disease takes about 20 years. So, we know, if we're going to intervene before you've lost any brain cells and before you've got memory loss, we need to be intervening much earlier than we are now.
(referring to an image) And this is an Alzheimer's diseased brain. You can see lots of holes - lots of cell loss. Really wide ventricles. And we know that this occurs over a great many years. If we were to intervene, say, 10 years before, we would expect still some cell loss, but as you can see here, there's a lot more of this white matter. If we were to intervene 20, 30 years before disease, we would hope to maintain full cell function and cells without the loss. And that's why early intervention is just so important.

NARRATION
In midlife, Graham Plant is doing just that. After his mother died from Alzheimer's in 2013, Graham decided to take active steps to try to avoid his mother's fate.

Graham Plant
And so that became a clarity point to say, "Well, what are the processes or things I can do to reduce the risk?" And at that point, I probably recognised that I wasn't overly healthy - I was a fair bit overweight - and sort of decided, "Well, it's time to make a change."
I almost classify running as not a hobby now - it's becoming a way of life. It's resulted in me being better in a whole host of ways as far as health and wellbeing.

NARRATION
Science is suggesting Graham's on the right track, because the genetic risk for Alzheimer's is actually less than you might think.

Prof Ralph Martins
There's a small percentage - less than 1% - of people who have a genetic form of Alzheimer's that causes Alzheimer's.

NARRATION
That's the uncommon, familial form of early-onset Alzheimer's. For the more prevalent later-onset form of the disease, the riskiest gene variant is APOE4. But even then, environmental factors will largely determine whether the disease develops.

Prof Ralph Martins
Now, genetic risk factors don't cause Alzheimer's disease, but together with other factors such as lifestyle factors, that's when people go over the edge and develop Alzheimer's disease.

Prof Cassandra Szoeke
We also know that the genetic component to risk appears to be only about a quarter. So that means that three-quarters of the risk is environmental and something that we can change.

NARRATION
It's an encouraging message, and exactly what we should be doing has been the focus of Professor Szoeke's latest research. She's trying to identify the preventative factors for cognitive decline.

Researcher
If I can just get you to lift up your arms for me.

NARRATION
Her team has followed a group of 400 women in Melbourne. When the study began, the women were aged between 45 and 55. They were then monitored for the next 20 years. A wide range of assessments were done, from physical measures, like their weight and BMI, to a battery of neuro-psychiatric tests.

Researcher
The first task I'm going to get you to do is a reaction time task.

NARRATION
Recruiting participants in midlife was pivotal.

Prof Cassandra Szoeke
A lot of the studies that look at cognitive decline in dementia recruit participants over 60 or over 70, because this is when cognitive decline in dementia starts to occur.

Researcher
I'm going to ask you to repeat as many of the words as you can remember.

Participant
Giraffe. Cow. Truck. Spinach...

Prof Cassandra Szoeke
One of the great things about our work was we were able to look at what people were doing at 45 to 55 and then look at cognitive decline across 15 years and see what factors were most important.

NARRATION
They found that the most important preventative factors against cognitive decline were having normal blood pressure and high levels of good cholesterol. But at number one was being physically active.

Prof Cassandra Szoeke
So, the results that are in the paper are the entire group, and they're group trends. What we're looking at here is individual people's test results.
(referring to a graph) So, this is someone who was exercising every day, and they remembered eight words and then they remembered as many words as possible - so, they hit what we call the ceiling of the test. They could not get better than this over time. This is another person who was exercising on average daily, and again, we can see quite good memory recollection, and maintained across all of the years of the study.
We look here at someone who's never exercised, and they have a poor memory function, and it declines quite considerably over the testing period. Another person, and again we see a memory decline over this period.
What we found was that the effect was cumulative. So, this meant that what you did for that entire 20 years was important for the memory you had in later life.

NARRATION
It seems a very clear message - move, often, and start today.

Prof Cassandra Szoeke
In this study, we were not prescriptive about what kind of physical activity you had to do - it was just being active on a daily basis.

NARRATION
Professor Szoeke's research was solely in women and only observational. The scientific gold standard, however, are randomised control trials, and American neuroscientist Kirk Erickson has conducted several of these trials in older adults with both women and men, looking at the effect of moderate exercise on brain size and memory. The 2011 trial was particularly provocative. 150 relatively inactive people were allocated to either an aerobic walking group or a stretching control group, and it was for a year.

Trainer
Extend your right leg to the ceiling with your toe pointed at the ceiling...

Prof Kirk Erickson
They come in for the same amount of time - three days per week, so the main differences between our two groups is the intensity of the activity. The walking group is getting moderate intensity and the stretching and toning more light intensity.

NARRATION
Before the participants began their activities, their brains were imaged.

Prof Kirk Erickson
We put them into an MRI machine, a magnetic resonance imaging machine, that allows us to take very high-resolution, detailed images of their brain.

NARRATION
They were particularly focusing on the hippocampus - a region critical to memory formation.

Prof Kirk Erickson
So, if you stick your fingers in your ears and...essentially like this - pointing at your ears, like this - you're essentially pointing at the hippocampus. So, the hippocampus sits behind the ears, deeper in the centre of the brain.

NARRATION
Normal ageing sees a decline in the size of the hippocampus of about 1% to 2% a year after the age of 50. Astoundingly, this trial found that brisk walking could reverse that decline.

Prof Kirk Erickson
(referring to a graph) In the red line, we're seeing a pattern of normal ageing. This is our control group that is showing a normal decline. In the blue line, we're seeing those people that are exercising. The exercising group showed an increase in the size of this structure over this one-year period. The change in the size of this structure amounted to about a 2% increase in the hippocampus - kind of like rolling back the clock about one to two years in terms of ageing of the hippocampus.

NARRATION
Whether these very tangible changes to the structure of the brain translate into improved cognitive function is yet to be fully established. But Kirk certainly believes they do.

Prof Kirk Erickson
We know that the hippocampus is involved in memory formation. We know that exercise influences the hippocampus. And we know that deterioration of the hippocampus happens with age and leads to Alzheimer's disease. So, there's plenty of reasons that enlarging the hippocampus through exercise will have a very clinical and meaningful impact on memory function and risk for dementia.

NARRATION
Graham Plant is moving much more than his mother did. He's also eating very differently to her.

Graham Plant
Her lemon slice and jelly slices were legendary. The Country Women's Association book of baking is kind of what she did. But, yeah, she loved being in the kitchen.

NARRATION
As does Graham. But these days, he's cooking a very different cuisine to the one he grew up on.

Graham Plant
Make the dressing, we'll whack the spuds...
She had a variety of tastes that she liked, but, no, niçoise salad wouldn't have been on, um...on the Country Women's Association cooking book, I don't think.

NARRATION
It's a diet he believes is better for his brain and health in general.

Graham Plant
I love cooking and I used to do a lot of barbecuing, a lot of...yeah, loads and loads of meat, whereas probably now, I don't really have any. Still fish. The fish side of things is one I keep as part of my protein intake. Twofold, as one is the oils are good for me, and there's a whole host of benefits around fish. But primarily vegetable. No dairy. And it's helped on...I guess reduced my weight, but also too, I feel better for it.

NARRATION
There's been plenty of research over the years showing the cardiovascular benefits of a healthy diet. Now there's mounting evidence diet also impacts on the brain and cognitive function.
Much of the research has looked at the Mediterranean diet, and one of those investigations is the Australian Imaging, Biomarkers and Lifestyle study, known as the AIBL study. It investigated the effect of a Western diet versus a Mediterranean diet on cognitive change in a group of 500 people.

Prof Ralph Martins
The AIBL study, which is a longitudinal study over the last eight years, we've been able to look at diet, and what we clearly show is that people who adhere very strongly to a Mediterranean diet have a lower risk of Alzheimer's and there's a lot lower levels of beta-amyloid in their brain.

NARRATION
Although the AIBL study is not a gold-standard clinical trial, its findings are consistent with other similar studies.

Prof Cassandra Szoeke
Adherence to a Mediterranean diet means you're more likely to have good executive functioning, which is what we call planning, and that a Western diet is more likely to drop your visuospatial. And these kind of things are associated with a vascular disease, which is expected for a Western diet.

Sue Radd
(leading a cooking class) The first dish I'm going to make is a very traditional village-style vegetable stew...

NARRATION
Sue Radd is a dietitian and an expert in the Mediterranean diet.

Sue Radd
(To class) Most dishes in the Mediterranean start off with...garlic, onion and olive oil.
What we're currently lacking is good-quality clinical trials on the Mediterranean diet and cognition and brain function. So this, I think, is going to be the next frontier, but we have reason to be optimistic. Because the Mediterranean diet, generally speaking, is also associated with a longer life span.
(To class) And everything goes into one pot. This is what I love about this dish.

NARRATION
The 'Mediterranean diet' refers to the cuisine consumed in the olive-growing regions around the Mediterranean Sea. It's a culturally broad and diverse area.

Sue Radd
So it's not exactly identical, say, in Lebanon or Morocco or Spain, but what is characterising the Mediterranean diet is that it is a plant-based diet based on unrefined foods - so, lots of whole grains, legumes, fruits and vegetables, nuts and seeds, and of course, extra-virgin olive oil.
(To class) What olive oil does is it sweetens the vegetables, so even bitter-tasting vegetables, such as those edible wild greens, can be masked, the bitterness can be masked, and the olive oil makes the vegies taste really sweet.

NARRATION
The extent to which each ingredient in the diet is protective against Alzheimer's isn't yet clear.

Prof Ralph Martins
We think two particular ingredients have very, very powerful roles to play. One is fish, and we think omega-3s in fish are gonna be big players, and fruit and vegetables - so, a lot of the anti-oxidants you'd find in fruit and vegetables.

Sue Radd
(To class) What we've done, we have thoroughly washed our dark leafy greens - endive, in this case - and we're just going to stuff those, as many as we can, into a pot...
So, with the dark green leafy vegetables, what we know at present, with scientific research, is that they're very rich in something called lutein. Lutein is an important anti-oxidant that gets deposited in the back of the eye, the macula, and it's a bit like sunscreen for the eye. But also, it gets taken up into the brain, where it's concentrated, and we believe it may have an important role there as an anti-oxidant.
(To class) They call this 'horta'. 'Horta' means...'grass'.
These dark green leafy vegetables are loaded in something called nitrate. Nitrate, when consumed, gets converted into the body into nitric oxide, and nitric oxide is crucial to helping keep your blood vessels flexible. And that's important as we get older, because blood vessels tend to stiffen up.
(To class) Does anyone need more olive oil?

Class participant
I can taste it.

Sue Radd
You can taste it? Fantastic.

NARRATION
Another thing about the Mediterranean diet is it's low in refined sugar.

Sue Radd
The traditional Mediterranean diet was very low in added sugar content. That was because they had to buy it and people were poor in those times. So if anything was used for sweeteners, it was either a bit of honey or a bit of grape must or something like that. But the diet was generally low-sugar.

NARRATION
Striking sugar off the menu is a challenge for many. Like Susan Lynch , a participant in the AIBL study.

Susan Lynch
The hardest part of trying to follow the Mediterranean diet is cutting out all the cakes and biscuits and ice-creams, and that really is difficult - for me.

NARRATION
The excessive sugar intake in the Western diet increases the risk of developing insulin resistance. This is essentially when the action of the body's insulin becomes ineffective.
Some researchers, like Professor Suzanne de la Monte, believe this has a detrimental effect on the brain, leading to a type of brain diabetes and eventually Alzheimer's.

Prof Suzanne de la Monte
People have gradually increased the interest in the brain diabetes story, and I think it's a very exciting time to be doing this type of research.

NARRATION
Insulin is a hormone best known for controlling the amount of blood glucose in the body, but it wasn't until Professor de la Monte began researching that she realised insulin has a crucial role in the brain too. It aids the uptake of glucose in the brain's nerve cells and helps regulate the chemicals involved in the brain's signalling.

Prof Suzanne de la Monte
I knew that insulin had an effect on keeping neurons alive, and at the time I was studying it, there was actually no information, so I was the beginning of studying how insulin worked in the brain.

NARRATION
To begin with, Professor de la Monte's team blocked the action of insulin in the brains of rats to see if it had any effect. The results were profound.

Prof Suzanne de la Monte
So, the way we test the animals - we put them in a maze. It's called a water maze. And they're supposed to be able to learn where the platform is, and they swim until they find the platform. And the smarter they are, they quickly recognise where the platform is, even if they can't see it.
But the rats that lose their hippocampal function because we knocked out the insulin receptor or we knocked out insulin, they spend a longer time looking for the platform, they don't remember where it was, and they're very slow and sloppy at learning.

NARRATION
These rats had developed amyloid-like plaques resembling the ones found in people with Alzheimer's.

Prof Suzanne de la Monte
Many of the features that we look for in Alzheimer's were present in these animals, and I think that helped to fortify the hypothesis that Alzheimer's is a metabolic disease, very similar to diabetes, but pretty much confined to the brain.

NARRATION
It is a tempting thesis. But to researchers like Professor Szoeke, Alzheimer's prevention likely involves more than one factor. It's about combination.

Prof Cassandra Szoeke
I think also when we look at diet and exercise and a lot of these factors, social engagement, all these things we need to do, we forget about the overlaps between them. So, with physical activity, those people who are doing more physical activity, often it was in group activities. Or even when they're going for a walk, they're going for a walk with someone else. So there are added benefits more than just the exercise on its own.

NARRATION
That combination of lifestyle interventions on cognitive function is the focus of this randomised control trial. It's being conducted by a team of sleep scientists in Melbourne.

Assoc Prof Clare Anderson
So, diet, exercise and sleep are considered the three pillars of health, and based on research in the sleep field, we know that maintaining good-quality sleep is key to maintaining cognitive function in later life.

Jessy Manousakis
OK, so, for this task, you're going to be trying to find a hidden pathway through a maze.

Participant
(chuckles) Oh, dear. I'm stuck!

Jessy Manousakis
So, we're looking to see whether enriching someone's lifestyle improves both their sleep and their memory, and then we're looking to see whether those improvements are related to each other - so, whether by improving sleep, you can also improve memory.

NARRATION
The intervention involves what they call an enriched environment. It features three different activities, and they're done in a group. There's a creative class, like painting, a cognitive activity, like chess, and an exercise class.

Art teacher
Because you've used other colours that are in your painting, there's more of a harmony, colour harmony.

NARRATION
Up to now, most of the lifestyle intervention studies have isolated each of the interventions.

Jessy Manousakis
They generally never combine the activities together. However, animal research has shown that by combining these things together, you get greater improvements.

Assoc Prof Clare Anderson
We suspect that the total of those is greater than the sum of its parts. So by combining them, we hope to alleviate more the cognitive symptomology of these individuals.

NARRATION
Sleep is essential for a host of reasons, including for brain function. Recently, we've learnt that one specific stage of sleep is critical for memory formation.

Assoc Prof Clare Anderson
We know this because if we deprive an individual of slow-wave sleep, memory is severely impacted, and if we enhance slow-wave sleep, we enhance memory performance.

NARRATION
But as you age, you spend much less time in that memory-forming slow-wave sleep phase, as you can see in this comparison of an older and younger person.

Assoc Prof Clare Anderson
(referring to a graph) So, this represents an eight-hour sleep period for N1 sleep, N2 sleep, which are lighter stages of sleep, and the slow-wave sleep, which is represented here by the blue bar. We can see for the first sleep cycle there's a low of slow-wave sleep in this younger participant, and also in the second sleep cycle as well. If we compare this to the older participant, and again, looking at the blue bar, you can see that there's much less duration of slow-wave sleep.

NARRATION
The team is hoping the combination of lifestyle activities will have a positive effect on slow-wave sleep, and in turn, on memory.

Jessy Manousakis
Because the study is ongoing, we haven't analysed all of the data at this point, but we have had a look at some initial results and they are promising. So, we've seen that there is an improvement in self-reported memory.

NARRATION
We've long known that healthy ageing is possible, though far from inevitable. But we now know Alzheimer's isn't just a lottery.

Prof Kirk Erickson
I don't think anyone in this field is saying that participation in physical activity or eating a healthy diet will eliminate your risk. There's always gonna be a risk, right? No matter how healthy you are, no matter what you do, there's always gonna be a risk for heart disease or cancer or dementia. So we can't be 100% certain ever. But I think that if we can cut your risk in half, that's pretty substantial, that's pretty significant.

NARRATION
Making the right choices throughout life increases the odds of a good old age. That benefits ourselves, our families and society at large.

Graham Plant
Alzheimer's, it's terrible for the person. It's equally as bad for the family. And so I would hate to think I'd put my family through that as a consequence of poor maintenance.

Prof Cassandra Szoeke
I certainly believe we can delay the onset of Alzheimer's disease. Without a doubt. Now.

Graham Plant
A lot of little things together actually make a big difference. I mean, a little bit of diet, a little bit of exercise - you don't have to do a lot. Then it all starts to come together and you feel much better for it.

NARRATION Graham Plant grew up in country Victoria. As a young man, he was close to his mum, Cathy. Graham Plant She lived for the family and the kids, and that was what really drove her, and she was happiest when the family was around her. NARRATION But about 10 years ago, Cathy Plant developed Alzheimer's. She was in her late 60s. Graham Plant It was kind of a slow onset, and then as it got slightly worse, she started to forget things that she was good at, like cooking, or she'd just forget to do things altogether, or she just got disoriented. Like putting the electric kettle on the hotplate, and things like that, and forgetting what can go in the oven and what can't, and those sort of things. When people get diagnosed with dementia, Alzheimer's, you lose them long before they go. That's kind of the way it is. NARRATION Alzheimer's disease is the most common form of dementia, accounting for up to 70% of cases. The condition is chronic, degenerative and ultimately terminal. Prof Cassandra Szoeke So, the hallmarks of the disease, clinically speaking, is memory loss and change in brain function. For some of the dementias, this can be other brain functions than memory, but for Alzheimer's disease, the first changes noticed are memory. NARRATION In a healthy brain, billions of neurons send messages to each other via electrical or chemical signals down a long tail - an axon. These are the synaptic connections through which messages travel. But in the Alzheimer's brain, toxic deposits accumulate, including a protein called beta-amyloid. The amyloid seems to attract another brain protein called tau to form fibrous clumps inside brain cells. This disturbs the brain's message transport system and neural networks effectively disintegrate. Until recently, this characteristic accumulation of beta-amyloid was only detectable after death in a post-mortem. But thanks largely to Australian research, with advanced imaging, it can now be seen in the living. It turns out the process of accumulation can begin several decades before Alzheimer's disease appears. Prof Cassandra Szoeke To get from a normal amount to the amount in people with Alzheimer's disease takes about 20 years. So, we know, if we're going to intervene before you've lost any brain cells and before you've got memory loss, we need to be intervening much earlier than we are now. (referring to an image) And this is an Alzheimer's diseased brain. You can see lots of holes - lots of cell loss. Really wide ventricles. And we know that this occurs over a great many years. If we were to intervene, say, 10 years before, we would expect still some cell loss, but as you can see here, there's a lot more of this white matter. If we were to intervene 20, 30 years before disease, we would hope to maintain full cell function and cells without the loss. And that's why early intervention is just so important. NARRATION In midlife, Graham Plant is doing just that. After his mother died from Alzheimer's in 2013, Graham decided to take active steps to try to avoid his mother's fate. Graham Plant And so that became a clarity point to say, "Well, what are the processes or things I can do to reduce the risk?" And at that point, I probably recognised that I wasn't overly healthy - I was a fair bit overweight - and sort of decided, "Well, it's time to make a change." I almost classify running as not a hobby now - it's becoming a way of life. It's resulted in me being better in a whole host of ways as far as health and wellbeing. NARRATION Science is suggesting Graham's on the right track, because the genetic risk for Alzheimer's is actually less than you might think. Prof Ralph Martins There's a small percentage - less than 1% - of people who have a genetic form of Alzheimer's that causes Alzheimer's. NARRATION That's the uncommon, familial form of early-onset Alzheimer's. For the more prevalent later-onset form of the disease, the riskiest gene variant is APOE4. But even then, environmental factors will largely determine whether the disease develops. Prof Ralph Martins Now, genetic risk factors don't cause Alzheimer's disease, but together with other factors such as lifestyle factors, that's when people go over the edge and develop Alzheimer's disease. Prof Cassandra Szoeke We also know that the genetic component to risk appears to be only about a quarter. So that means that three-quarters of the risk is environmental and something that we can change. NARRATION It's an encouraging message, and exactly what we should be doing has been the focus of Professor Szoeke's latest research. She's trying to identify the preventative factors for cognitive decline. Researcher If I can just get you to lift up your arms for me. NARRATION Her team has followed a group of 400 women in Melbourne. When the study began, the women were aged between 45 and 55. They were then monitored for the next 20 years. A wide range of assessments were done, from physical measures, like their weight and BMI, to a battery of neuro-psychiatric tests. Researcher The first task I'm going to get you to do is a reaction time task. NARRATION Recruiting participants in midlife was pivotal. Prof Cassandra Szoeke A lot of the studies that look at cognitive decline in dementia recruit participants over 60 or over 70, because this is when cognitive decline in dementia starts to occur. Researcher I'm going to ask you to repeat as many of the words as you can remember. Participant Giraffe. Cow. Truck. Spinach... Prof Cassandra Szoeke One of the great things about our work was we were able to look at what people were doing at 45 to 55 and then look at cognitive decline across 15 years and see what factors were most important. NARRATION They found that the most important preventative factors against cognitive decline were having normal blood pressure and high levels of good cholesterol. But at number one was being physically active. Prof Cassandra Szoeke So, the results that are in the paper are the entire group, and they're group trends. What we're looking at here is individual people's test results. (referring to a graph) So, this is someone who was exercising every day, and they remembered eight words and then they remembered as many words as possible - so, they hit what we call the ceiling of the test. They could not get better than this over time. This is another person who was exercising on average daily, and again, we can see quite good memory recollection, and maintained across all of the years of the study. We look here at someone who's never exercised, and they have a poor memory function, and it declines quite considerably over the testing period. Another person, and again we see a memory decline over this period. What we found was that the effect was cumulative. So, this meant that what you did for that entire 20 years was important for the memory you had in later life. NARRATION It seems a very clear message - move, often, and start today. Prof Cassandra Szoeke In this study, we were not prescriptive about what kind of physical activity you had to do - it was just being active on a daily basis. NARRATION Professor Szoeke's research was solely in women and only observational. The scientific gold standard, however, are randomised control trials, and American neuroscientist Kirk Erickson has conducted several of these trials in older adults with both women and men, looking at the effect of moderate exercise on brain size and memory. The 2011 trial was particularly provocative. 150 relatively inactive people were allocated to either an aerobic walking group or a stretching control group, and it was for a year. Trainer Extend your right leg to the ceiling with your toe pointed at the ceiling... Prof Kirk Erickson They come in for the same amount of time - three days per week, so the main differences between our two groups is the intensity of the activity. The walking group is getting moderate intensity and the stretching and toning more light intensity. NARRATION Before the participants began their activities, their brains were imaged. Prof Kirk Erickson We put them into an MRI machine, a magnetic resonance imaging machine, that allows us to take very high-resolution, detailed images of their brain. NARRATION They were particularly focusing on the hippocampus - a region critical to memory formation. Prof Kirk Erickson So, if you stick your fingers in your ears and...essentially like this - pointing at your ears, like this - you're essentially pointing at the hippocampus. So, the hippocampus sits behind the ears, deeper in the centre of the brain. NARRATION Normal ageing sees a decline in the size of the hippocampus of about 1% to 2% a year after the age of 50. Astoundingly, this trial found that brisk walking could reverse that decline. Prof Kirk Erickson (referring to a graph) In the red line, we're seeing a pattern of normal ageing. This is our control group that is showing a normal decline. In the blue line, we're seeing those people that are exercising. The exercising group showed an increase in the size of this structure over this one-year period. The change in the size of this structure amounted to about a 2% increase in the hippocampus - kind of like rolling back the clock about one to two years in terms of ageing of the hippocampus. NARRATION Whether these very tangible changes to the structure of the brain translate into improved cognitive function is yet to be fully established. But Kirk certainly believes they do. Prof Kirk Erickson We know that the hippocampus is involved in memory formation. We know that exercise influences the hippocampus. And we know that deterioration of the hippocampus happens with age and leads to Alzheimer's disease. So, there's plenty of reasons that enlarging the hippocampus through exercise will have a very clinical and meaningful impact on memory function and risk for dementia. NARRATION Graham Plant is moving much more than his mother did. He's also eating very differently to her. Graham Plant Her lemon slice and jelly slices were legendary. The Country Women's Association book of baking is kind of what she did. But, yeah, she loved being in the kitchen. NARRATION As does Graham. But these days, he's cooking a very different cuisine to the one he grew up on. Graham Plant Make the dressing, we'll whack the spuds... She had a variety of tastes that she liked, but, no, niçoise salad wouldn't have been on, um...on the Country Women's Association cooking book, I don't think. NARRATION It's a diet he believes is better for his brain and health in general. Graham Plant I love cooking and I used to do a lot of barbecuing, a lot of...yeah, loads and loads of meat, whereas probably now, I don't really have any. Still fish. The fish side of things is one I keep as part of my protein intake. Twofold, as one is the oils are good for me, and there's a whole host of benefits around fish. But primarily vegetable. No dairy. And it's helped on...I guess reduced my weight, but also too, I feel better for it. NARRATION There's been plenty of research over the years showing the cardiovascular benefits of a healthy diet. Now there's mounting evidence diet also impacts on the brain and cognitive function. Much of the research has looked at the Mediterranean diet, and one of those investigations is the Australian Imaging, Biomarkers and Lifestyle study, known as the AIBL study. It investigated the effect of a Western diet versus a Mediterranean diet on cognitive change in a group of 500 people. Prof Ralph Martins The AIBL study, which is a longitudinal study over the last eight years, we've been able to look at diet, and what we clearly show is that people who adhere very strongly to a Mediterranean diet have a lower risk of Alzheimer's and there's a lot lower levels of beta-amyloid in their brain. NARRATION Although the AIBL study is not a gold-standard clinical trial, its findings are consistent with other similar studies. Prof Cassandra Szoeke Adherence to a Mediterranean diet means you're more likely to have good executive functioning, which is what we call planning, and that a Western diet is more likely to drop your visuospatial. And these kind of things are associated with a vascular disease, which is expected for a Western diet. Sue Radd (leading a cooking class) The first dish I'm going to make is a very traditional village-style vegetable stew... NARRATION Sue Radd is a dietitian and an expert in the Mediterranean diet. Sue Radd (To class) Most dishes in the Mediterranean start off with...garlic, onion and olive oil. What we're currently lacking is good-quality clinical trials on the Mediterranean diet and cognition and brain function. So this, I think, is going to be the next frontier, but we have reason to be optimistic. Because the Mediterranean diet, generally speaking, is also associated with a longer life span. (To class) And everything goes into one pot. This is what I love about this dish. NARRATION The 'Mediterranean diet' refers to the cuisine consumed in the olive-growing regions around the Mediterranean Sea. It's a culturally broad and diverse area. Sue Radd So it's not exactly identical, say, in Lebanon or Morocco or Spain, but what is characterising the Mediterranean diet is that it is a plant-based diet based on unrefined foods - so, lots of whole grains, legumes, fruits and vegetables, nuts and seeds, and of course, extra-virgin olive oil. (To class) What olive oil does is it sweetens the vegetables, so even bitter-tasting vegetables, such as those edible wild greens, can be masked, the bitterness can be masked, and the olive oil makes the vegies taste really sweet. NARRATION The extent to which each ingredient in the diet is protective against Alzheimer's isn't yet clear. Prof Ralph Martins We think two particular ingredients have very, very powerful roles to play. One is fish, and we think omega-3s in fish are gonna be big players, and fruit and vegetables - so, a lot of the anti-oxidants you'd find in fruit and vegetables. Sue Radd (To class) What we've done, we have thoroughly washed our dark leafy greens - endive, in this case - and we're just going to stuff those, as many as we can, into a pot... So, with the dark green leafy vegetables, what we know at present, with scientific research, is that they're very rich in something called lutein. Lutein is an important anti-oxidant that gets deposited in the back of the eye, the macula, and it's a bit like sunscreen for the eye. But also, it gets taken up into the brain, where it's concentrated, and we believe it may have an important role there as an anti-oxidant. (To class) They call this 'horta'. 'Horta' means...'grass'. These dark green leafy vegetables are loaded in something called nitrate. Nitrate, when consumed, gets converted into the body into nitric oxide, and nitric oxide is crucial to helping keep your blood vessels flexible. And that's important as we get older, because blood vessels tend to stiffen up. (To class) Does anyone need more olive oil? Class participant I can taste it. Sue Radd You can taste it? Fantastic. NARRATION Another thing about the Mediterranean diet is it's low in refined sugar. Sue Radd The traditional Mediterranean diet was very low in added sugar content. That was because they had to buy it and people were poor in those times. So if anything was used for sweeteners, it was either a bit of honey or a bit of grape must or something like that. But the diet was generally low-sugar. NARRATION Striking sugar off the menu is a challenge for many. Like Susan Lynch , a participant in the AIBL study. Susan Lynch The hardest part of trying to follow the Mediterranean diet is cutting out all the cakes and biscuits and ice-creams, and that really is difficult - for me. NARRATION The excessive sugar intake in the Western diet increases the risk of developing insulin resistance. This is essentially when the action of the body's insulin becomes ineffective. Some researchers, like Professor Suzanne de la Monte, believe this has a detrimental effect on the brain, leading to a type of brain diabetes and eventually Alzheimer's. Prof Suzanne de la Monte People have gradually increased the interest in the brain diabetes story, and I think it's a very exciting time to be doing this type of research. NARRATION Insulin is a hormone best known for controlling the amount of blood glucose in the body, but it wasn't until Professor de la Monte began researching that she realised insulin has a crucial role in the brain too. It aids the uptake of glucose in the brain's nerve cells and helps regulate the chemicals involved in the brain's signalling. Prof Suzanne de la Monte I knew that insulin had an effect on keeping neurons alive, and at the time I was studying it, there was actually no information, so I was the beginning of studying how insulin worked in the brain. NARRATION To begin with, Professor de la Monte's team blocked the action of insulin in the brains of rats to see if it had any effect. The results were profound. Prof Suzanne de la Monte So, the way we test the animals - we put them in a maze. It's called a water maze. And they're supposed to be able to learn where the platform is, and they swim until they find the platform. And the smarter they are, they quickly recognise where the platform is, even if they can't see it. But the rats that lose their hippocampal function because we knocked out the insulin receptor or we knocked out insulin, they spend a longer time looking for the platform, they don't remember where it was, and they're very slow and sloppy at learning. NARRATION These rats had developed amyloid-like plaques resembling the ones found in people with Alzheimer's. Prof Suzanne de la Monte Many of the features that we look for in Alzheimer's were present in these animals, and I think that helped to fortify the hypothesis that Alzheimer's is a metabolic disease, very similar to diabetes, but pretty much confined to the brain. NARRATION It is a tempting thesis. But to researchers like Professor Szoeke, Alzheimer's prevention likely involves more than one factor. It's about combination. Prof Cassandra Szoeke I think also when we look at diet and exercise and a lot of these factors, social engagement, all these things we need to do, we forget about the overlaps between them. So, with physical activity, those people who are doing more physical activity, often it was in group activities. Or even when they're going for a walk, they're going for a walk with someone else. So there are added benefits more than just the exercise on its own. NARRATION That combination of lifestyle interventions on cognitive function is the focus of this randomised control trial. It's being conducted by a team of sleep scientists in Melbourne. Assoc Prof Clare Anderson So, diet, exercise and sleep are considered the three pillars of health, and based on research in the sleep field, we know that maintaining good-quality sleep is key to maintaining cognitive function in later life. Jessy Manousakis OK, so, for this task, you're going to be trying to find a hidden pathway through a maze. Participant (chuckles) Oh, dear. I'm stuck! Jessy Manousakis So, we're looking to see whether enriching someone's lifestyle improves both their sleep and their memory, and then we're looking to see whether those improvements are related to each other - so, whether by improving sleep, you can also improve memory. NARRATION The intervention involves what they call an enriched environment. It features three different activities, and they're done in a group. There's a creative class, like painting, a cognitive activity, like chess, and an exercise class. Art teacher Because you've used other colours that are in your painting, there's more of a harmony, colour harmony. NARRATION Up to now, most of the lifestyle intervention studies have isolated each of the interventions. Jessy Manousakis They generally never combine the activities together. However, animal research has shown that by combining these things together, you get greater improvements. Assoc Prof Clare Anderson We suspect that the total of those is greater than the sum of its parts. So by combining them, we hope to alleviate more the cognitive symptomology of these individuals. NARRATION Sleep is essential for a host of reasons, including for brain function. Recently, we've learnt that one specific stage of sleep is critical for memory formation. Assoc Prof Clare Anderson We know this because if we deprive an individual of slow-wave sleep, memory is severely impacted, and if we enhance slow-wave sleep, we enhance memory performance. NARRATION But as you age, you spend much less time in that memory-forming slow-wave sleep phase, as you can see in this comparison of an older and younger person. Assoc Prof Clare Anderson (referring to a graph) So, this represents an eight-hour sleep period for N1 sleep, N2 sleep, which are lighter stages of sleep, and the slow-wave sleep, which is represented here by the blue bar. We can see for the first sleep cycle there's a low of slow-wave sleep in this younger participant, and also in the second sleep cycle as well. If we compare this to the older participant, and again, looking at the blue bar, you can see that there's much less duration of slow-wave sleep. NARRATION The team is hoping the combination of lifestyle activities will have a positive effect on slow-wave sleep, and in turn, on memory. Jessy Manousakis Because the study is ongoing, we haven't analysed all of the data at this point, but we have had a look at some initial results and they are promising. So, we've seen that there is an improvement in self-reported memory. NARRATION We've long known that healthy ageing is possible, though far from inevitable. But we now know Alzheimer's isn't just a lottery. Prof Kirk Erickson I don't think anyone in this field is saying that participation in physical activity or eating a healthy diet will eliminate your risk. There's always gonna be a risk, right? No matter how healthy you are, no matter what you do, there's always gonna be a risk for heart disease or cancer or dementia. So we can't be 100% certain ever. But I think that if we can cut your risk in half, that's pretty substantial, that's pretty significant. NARRATION Making the right choices throughout life increases the odds of a good old age. That benefits ourselves, our families and society at large. Graham Plant Alzheimer's, it's terrible for the person. It's equally as bad for the family. And so I would hate to think I'd put my family through that as a consequence of poor maintenance. Prof Cassandra Szoeke I certainly believe we can delay the onset of Alzheimer's disease. Without a doubt. Now. Graham Plant A lot of little things together actually make a big difference. I mean, a little bit of diet, a little bit of exercise - you don't have to do a lot. Then it all starts to come together and you feel much better for it. metadata.Summary: It's said memory is the mother of all wisdom, a fundamental part of being human. But Alzheimer's disease slowly robs the mind. It's a cruel and undignified descent. Alzheimer's is the most common form of dementia, accounting for up to 70 per cent of cases. After the age of 65, the chance of getting the disease doubles every five years. Given there's no cure, it's scary stuff. But mounting research suggests that Alzheimer's can be delayed - and even prevented. In this episode we explore how lifestyle choices today may affect our chances of cognitive decline in the future. From what we eat to how much we move, even how we sleep ... scientists are suggesting that the power to push back the disease is largely in our hands.
